autoSwap.enabledDescription: Also switch the account new sessions start on, using the same limits.
autoSwap.sessionThresholdDescription: Swap away once the 5-hour window reaches this. 90% matches claude-swap.
autoSwap.weeklyThresholdDescription: Swap away once the weekly (or a per-model weekly) window reaches this.
autoSwap.hysteresisDescription: A swap target needs this many more points of headroom than the current account, and must be under its own limits, so swaps never bounce.
autoSwap.cooldownDescription: Minimum time between swaps before a limit. A full window or dead login skips it.
autoSwap.failoverDescription: Swap immediately when the current login expires or is revoked, and pause that account.
autoSwap.modelLimitsDescription: Treat a model-specific weekly cap like the weekly limit.
autoSwap.apiKeyFallbackDescription: Launch on a pay-as-you-go key when every subscription is exhausted.
autoSwap.liveSessionsDescription: Seal polls every account’s 5-hour and weekly usage and moves a running agent to another account before it crosses a limit below, or right away if its login dies. It resumes the conversation when it cannot switch live.
autoSwap.rateLimitFallbackDescription: Last resort only. If an agent stops with a usage-limit message that polling has not caught yet, move it anyway.
autoSwap.title: Auto-swap
autoSwap.description: Seal reads every account’s 5-hour and 7-day usage and moves work to the next account in the list before a limit is hit. Each provider has its own settings.

onboarding.title: Add your first account
onboarding.body: Seal runs Claude Code and Codex on the accounts you add here. With two or more, it watches each account’s 5-hour and 7-day usage and moves work to the next one before a limit stops you.
onboarding.step1: Add each subscription. Every sign-in gets a folder of its own, so accounts never overwrite each other.
onboarding.step2: Drag accounts into the order you prefer, and turn on auto-swap.
onboarding.step3: Optionally pin projects or machines to specific accounts with rules, and push logins to your other machines.

installDialog.serviceAuto: Seal registers a user service that keeps the server running: PM2 when the machine has PM2, otherwise a systemd user service. When the machine has neither, no service is registered, and the server starts when Seal connects and stops when idle.
installDialog.serviceSystemd: Seal registers a systemd user service that keeps the server running, as chosen under Advanced. When the machine cannot run one, Seal uses PM2 when the machine has it.
installDialog.servicePm2: Seal registers the server with PM2, which keeps it running, as chosen under Advanced. When the machine has no PM2, Seal registers a systemd user service instead.
installDialog.serviceLaunchd: Seal registers a launchd user service (experimental) that keeps the server running, as chosen under Advanced. launchd starts the server when you log in at the Mac’s screen, so the server does not run on a Mac nobody logs in to.
installDialog.linger: With systemd, Seal asks the machine to turn on lingering for your account, so the service keeps running after this computer disconnects.
installDialog.laterRemoval: Later, “Remove Seal server” stops the server and removes the service. Lingering stays on, and so do ~/.orca-remote, ~/.orca, ~/.claude/keybindings.json, ~/.claude/orca-agent-view.json and the status hooks in your coding agents’ settings.
installDialog.title: Install Seal server on {{name}}?
installDialog.files: Seal writes its server files to ~/.orca-remote on {{name}}, then connects to {{name}} through the server instead of plain SSH.
installDialog.moveAnyway: The saved items listed on this machine’s page stay on this computer and do not appear on {{name}}.
installDialog.serviceLaunchdFallback: When no one is logged in at the screen during the install, no service is registered, and the server starts when Seal connects and stops when idle. On a machine without launchd, Seal chooses as it does automatically: PM2 when the machine has PM2, otherwise a systemd user service.
installDialog.serverData: Once it runs, the server keeps its own data in ~/.orca (keys, its database and agent hook settings), writes ~/.claude/keybindings.json and ~/.claude/orca-agent-view.json, and adds its status hooks to the settings of the coding agents it finds on {{name}}.

keepRunningDialog.title: Keep Seal server running on {{name}} as a service?
keepRunningDialog.service: Seal registers the server that already runs on {{name}} as a user service and restarts the server once. The service is PM2 when the machine has PM2, otherwise a systemd user service.
keepRunningDialog.serviceLaunchd: Seal registers the server that already runs on {{name}} as a launchd user service (experimental) and restarts the server once. launchd starts the server when you log in at the Mac’s screen, so the server does not run on a Mac nobody logs in to. When no one is logged in at the screen now, no service is registered.

reuseDialog.title: Use the Seal server you set up on {{name}}?
reuseDialog.connects: Seal connects to {{name}} through the Seal server you set up there. Over SSH, Seal runs “seal pair” on {{name}} to get an access link from that server: if this computer is already paired with the server, Seal keeps that pairing, otherwise it pairs with the link. Seal adds its own SSH tunnel only when the pairing needs one and has none.
reuseDialog.nothingInstalled: Nothing is installed on {{name}}, and the server is not restarted.

remove.title: Remove Seal server from {{name}}?
remove.stops: This stops Seal server on {{name}} and removes its service. {{name}} goes back to a plain SSH connection, and projects and sessions opened through the server are no longer shown on this computer.
remove.stays: Lingering and your project files stay on the machine, and so do ~/.orca-remote, ~/.orca, ~/.claude/keybindings.json, ~/.claude/orca-agent-view.json and the status hooks in your coding agents’ settings.
remove.terminals: Running terminals block the removal: close the terminals that run through the server first.
